title: How to Read a PhD Job Advert: Funding, Eligibility and Application Steps
content:
Read a PhD advert as a set of conditions to check. Identify the scientific question, essential qualifications, funding package, location and submission process before investing time in the application.

This guide explains how to decode a PhD advertisement line by line, what to look for, and what red flags should make you think twice before applying.

Do not assume that an advert without a named supervisor is fraudulent: centrally recruited doctoral programmes can legitimately appoint supervisors later.

“I am applying as an international candidate. Does the advertised funding cover the full international tuition fee, or only the home-rate fee? Could you also confirm stipend or salary, funding duration and any mandatory employment duties?”

A Funding Question Worth Asking

Read the host institution’s original advertisement. A third-party board can help you discover vacancies, but only the official call can confirm eligibility, salary or studentship amount, nationality restrictions, contract status and deadline. Some calls accept international applicants but cover only domestic-rate tuition. Others offer employment rather than a studentship.

First Check Whether You Are Eligible

The Standard Structure of a PhD Advertisement

Most PhD adverts follow a similar structure, whether they are posted on a university website, FindAPhD, EURAXESS, or a national job board. Here is what each section typically contains.

SectionWhat It Tells You
TitleThe specific research area and often the project name
Host institution and departmentWhere you will work and which research group
Supervisor(s)Who will supervise you — read their recent papers
Project descriptionThe research question, methods, and expected outputs
EligibilityDegree requirements, nationality rules, English language
FundingWhat is covered — tuition, stipend, duration
Required documentsExactly what to submit and in what format
DeadlineWhen to apply — often strict, no extensions
ContactWho to email with questions — usually the supervisor

Section 1: Title and Project Name

The title tells you what the project is about. Read it carefully.

  • Broad titles ("PhD in Machine Learning") mean the supervisor may be flexible about the exact topic. This can be an advantage if you have your own idea.
  • Specific titles ("Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Contact Humanoid Locomotion") mean the project is already defined. You will need to show that you can contribute to that specific area.
  • Project names or acronyms (e.g. "PhD position in the HAMMER project") usually mean the project is funded by a grant with defined deliverables.

Section 2: Host Institution and Department

Check where the position is based. Some things to consider:

  • Is the department well-regarded in your field?
  • Is the location somewhere you want to live for 3-4 years?
  • Is the lab well-equipped with the resources you need?
  • Are there other researchers in your area at the same institution?

If the position is part of a Centre for Doctoral Training, a graduate school, or a consortium, note that — these often come with additional training, networking, and internship opportunities.

Section 3: Supervisor(s)

The supervisor is the most important person in your PhD. Before applying, do the following:

  • Read their recent publications. Look at the last 3-5 papers they have published.
  • Check their supervision record. How many PhD students have they supervised? Where are those students now?
  • Look at their funding. Are they actively funded? This matters because a funded project is more likely to be secure for the full duration.
  • Check their research group size. A large group means more peer support; a small group means more one-to-one attention.

Section 4: Project Description

This is where you learn what the project is actually about. Read carefully for:

  • Research question: What problem is the project trying to solve?
  • Methodology: What methods will you use? Simulation, laboratory work, fieldwork, data analysis, theory?
  • Expected outputs: Will the project produce publications, software, patents, or prototypes?
  • Collaboration: Does the project involve working with industry partners, other universities, or international collaborators?
  • Deliverables and milestones: Some projects have defined milestones, especially those funded by specific grants.

Section 5: Eligibility

This is where you find out whether you are allowed to apply. Read it very carefully — eligibility rules are strict, and applications that do not meet them are usually rejected automatically.

Degree Requirements

  • Do they require a Master's, or will they accept a Bachelor's?
  • What classification is required? First-Class, Upper Second (2:1), or equivalent?
  • Are there subject-specific requirements (e.g. "a degree in computer science, mathematics, or a related field")?

Nationality and Residency

  • Is the position open to international applicants, or is it restricted to UK/EU/home students?
  • Does the funding cover international fees, or only home fees?
  • Are there specific nationality requirements for visa sponsorship?

This is one of the most common reasons applicants waste time. If the advert says "Home students only", and you are an international applicant, you cannot apply unless you can self-fund.

English Language Requirements

  • What is the minimum IELTS or TOEFL score?
  • Will they accept a degree taught in English as evidence?
  • Are there specific band requirements (e.g. "IELTS 6.5 with no band below 6.0")?

Other Requirements

  • Do you need specific technical skills (programming languages, lab techniques)?
  • Do you need to have published before applying?
  • Are there age limits (rare, but occasionally present)?
  • Do you need an ATAS certificate (for certain UK science and engineering subjects)?

Section 6: Funding

This is where you learn what you are actually being offered. Read carefully for:

  • Tuition fees: Are fees covered, and at which rate (home or international)?
  • Stipend or salary: How much per year or month? Is it tax-free?
  • Duration: How many years is the funding guaranteed?
  • Additional support: Is there a research budget for conferences, equipment, or travel?
  • Conditions: Is there a probation period? Are there teaching requirements?

Common Funding Models

Funding ModelWhat It Means
Fully funded studentshipTuition + stipend + research budget
Tuition-only fundingFees covered, but you need to cover living costs
Stipend-only fundingLiving costs covered, but not fees
Employment contractYou are a salaried employee with social benefits
Self-fundedYou must cover everything yourself

Section 7: Required Documents

The advert will usually list exactly what you need to submit. Common documents include:

  • Academic CV
  • Cover letter or motivation letter
  • Research proposal (if required — check the word limit)
  • Academic transcripts and degree certificates
  • English language test certificate
  • Two or three references
  • Writing sample (for some humanities and social science programmes)
  • Portfolio (for design-related programmes)
  • Copy of passport

Follow the instructions exactly. If the advert says "PDF only", do not send a Word document. If it says "research proposal of 1,500 to 2,000 words", do not submit 5,000 words.

Section 8: Deadline and Application Process

  • Is the deadline fixed, or is it rolling until the position is filled?
  • How do you apply — via the university portal, by email to the supervisor, or through a specific system?
  • Are there any interviews, and how are they conducted?
  • When is the expected start date?

Deadlines are usually strict. Apply well before the deadline — some committees start reviewing applications as soon as they arrive.

Red Flags to Watch For

  • "Self-funded" without any mention of funding: If the advert does not mention any funding, assume none is available.
  • Vague project description: If the project is described in one sentence, it may not be well planned.
  • No named supervisor: A PhD without a named supervisor is unusual. Ask who will supervise you.
  • Extremely short deadlines: If the advert is posted with a deadline in a few days, it may have been posted late or the funding may be at risk.
  • Requests for payment: Legitimate PhD positions never ask you to pay for the position itself. Application fees are fine, but "registration fees" or "processing fees" are scams.
  • No contact person: A good advert always provides a contact for questions.

How to Tailor Your Application to the Advertisement

  1. Use the exact terms from the advert. If it says "reinforcement learning and control", use those words in your proposal and cover letter.
  2. Address each eligibility criterion explicitly. If they ask for experience with Python, say clearly that you have it and give an example.
  3. Reference the supervisor's work. Read one or two of their recent papers and mention how your background connects.
  4. Follow the format instructions exactly. Formatting mistakes make you look careless.
  5. Apply early. Many committees review applications as they arrive, and early applicants often have an advantage.

Checklist Before You Apply

ItemChecked?
I meet all eligibility requirements (degree, nationality, English)
I understand the funding — tuition, stipend, duration
I have read at least one paper by the supervisor
I have all the required documents ready
My research proposal matches the project described
I know the deadline and the application method
I have a contact email in case of questions

Before you submit

A PhD advertisement is a dense document, and every line matters. Read it carefully, take notes, and make sure you understand what is being offered before you invest hours in an application. Then tailor your CV, cover letter, and proposal to the specific project.

Browse PhD opportunities on NextApply — each listing shows the funding details, eligibility, and deadline so you can decide quickly whether the position is right for you.

Official Sources and Useful Links

  • EURAXESS jobs portal
  • NextApply opportunities

Always use the official admissions, funding or immigration page as the final authority before applying. NextApply is an opportunity discovery platform, not the admissions office.

Underline the words that change the decision

Read the advert once for the science and again for the conditions. Underline essential qualifications, fee-status restrictions, contract length, language requirements and the submission route. Check whether the deadline applies to the complete application or an initial expression of interest. If the funding details say Home fees, ask about the international difference. If the advert describes a fixed project, tailor your statement to that project rather than proposing an unrelated doctorate. Keep a copy of the instructions you used when preparing the application.

Relevant listings and guides on NextApply

To see how these questions apply to a real listing, review Fully Funded PhD Studentship in Foundational AI at University College London. Compare its stated requirements with your own preparation and check the official source before applying.

You can also browse University College London on NextApply and the PhD positions category. Listings and recruitment windows can change.
